[Borrowing Strength](https://arenamag.com/articles/borrowing-strength), by Alex
Kesin in Arena Magazine, October 2026.

**Population pharmacokinetics began with an economist's idea: estimate each
patient and the population together, so that one patient's sparse data borrows
strength from everyone else's.** Barr Rosenberg, a Harvard economist known for
forecasting financial risk, came to the problem while his mother was being
harmed by a miscalculated digoxin dose that kept rising as her health worsened.
He saw no real difference between the stock market and human metabolism: both
are hidden systems that have to be inferred from sparse, noisy data.

- **Borrowing strength.** A new patient starts on a dose drawn from the
  population, and the estimate moves toward that patient as their own blood
  levels come in. This is the mixed-effects model behind every population PK
  analysis.
- **Sheiner and NONMEM.** Rosenberg sketched the idea at a seminar at the
  University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) around 1969 to 1970. Lewis
  Sheiner and Stuart Beal built it into NONMEM there in the late 1970s, and
  the first version shipped in April 1980. Alison Boeckmann later added NM-TRAN
  and PREDPP.
- **Regulation.** Carl Peck carried the methods into the FDA. The article
  links them to Section 115a of the 1997 FDA Modernization Act, which lets
  one adequate, well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence, including
  pharmacokinetic data, establish that a drug works.
- **Rosenberg's two careers.** His financial career was celebrated, and it ended in
  a lifetime ban from the industry, after he concealed a coding error in his
  firm's risk model. His role in founding pharmacometrics is largely
  forgotten.
